metadata.title: OBLIVIATOR: OBLIVIous Parallel Joins and other OperATORs in Shared Memory Environments
metadata.description:
This is the artifact repository of Obliviator. Our work is in full accordance with the USENIX'25 ethics guidelines. We propose new algorithms and implement systems with a positive impact on preserving data privacy. Our experiments involved neither testing on live systems without prior consent, nor human participants.

All our tests were executed either on synthetic datasets whose creation we describe or on already publicly available real-world datasets. They include TPC-H, a synthesized benchmark with created contents, a twitter social graph that is available to the public and contains the anonymized topology of the Twitter social network (also used in [1, 2, 3]), a public IMDb dataset that contains the public information of title names and actors (used in [4, 5]), a public Amazon dataset that records frequently co-purchased products (used in [5, 6]), a joke dataset that contains anonymous ratings of jokes by different users (used in [5, 7]), and slashdot dataset that contains technology news website with friend/foe links between users (used in [5, 8]). We would like to point out that none of these benchmarks/datasets can cause any type of harm and are strictly used to evaluate our algorithms.

Additionally, we open-source all artifacts required for recreating our algorithms and experiments. They include all our code in this paper, scripts to generate the synthesized dataset, scripts to process public benchmarks and datasets, configuration information, and scripts to reproduce our evaluation.

Please refer to ./document_availability.pdf for artifact evaluation phase-1, artifact availability.

Please refer to ./artifact_appendix.pdf for artifact evaluation phase-2, artifact functionality.

Please feel free to Email for any troubleshooting. And here are some reminders:

To replicate our experiments of joins on real-world datasets, please disable the PRE_ALLOCATION flag in the Makefile and adjust the warmup size in scalable_oblivious_join.c to match the available EPC size. For convenience, please just use the join_real_world folder directly.

Also, please pay attention to the following settings:

1) Ensure that NumTCS is smaller than the number of available cores on your machine.
2) Typically, just set NumHeapPages and NumStackPages to be smaller than the total available EPC size on your machine. If the input and output sizes are too large, we can increase these values.
3) Make sure that MAX_BUF_SIZE in parallel.c is larger than the sizes of the input and output files.
4) The machine used for experiments in our paper is Standard_DC32ds_v3. For this machine, we set NumStackPages to be 262144.

V6 update: We attach the correct KKS* program for both the following two input formats: "key (integer) data (integer)" (e.g., for the synthesized dataset), and "key (integer) data (string)" (e.g., for TPC-H dataset).

References

[1] Meeyoung Cha, Hamed Haddadi, Fabricio Benevenuto, and Krishna P. Gummadi. Measuring User Influence in Twitter: The Million Follower Fallacy. In In Proceedings of the 4th International AAAI Conference on Weblogs and Social Media (ICWSM).

[2] Zhao Chang, Dong Xie, Sheng Wang, and Feifei Li. Towards practical oblivious join. In Proceedings of the 2022 International Conference on Management of Data. Association for Computing Machinery, 2022.

[3] Xiang Li, Nuozhou Sun, Yunqian Luo, and Mingyu Gao. Soda: A set of fast oblivious algorithms in distributed secure data analytics. Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, 16(7):1671–1684, 2023.

[4] Kevin Lewi and David J Wu. Order-revealing encryption: New constructions, applications, and lower bounds. In Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, pages 1167–1178, 2016.

[5] Shuyuan Li, Yuxiang Zeng, Yuxiang Wang, Yiman Zhong, Zimu Zhou, and Yongxin Tong. An experimental study on federated equi-joins. IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 2024.

[6] Jaewon Yang and Jure Leskovec. Defining and evaluating network communities based on ground-truth. In Proceedings of the ACM SIGKDD Workshop on Mining Data Semantics, pages 1–8, 2012.

[7] Ken Goldberg, Theresa Roeder, Dhruv Gupta, and Chris Perkins. Eigentaste: A constant time collaborative filtering algorithm. information retrieval, 4:133–151, 2001.

[8] Jure Leskovec, Daniel Huttenlocher, and Jon Kleinberg. Signed networks in social media. In Proceedings of the SIGCHI conference on human factors in computing systems, pages 1361–1370, 2010.

metadata.title: Leveraging ASIC AI Chips for Homomorphic Encryption
metadata.description:
This artifact presents CROSS, the first end-to-end framework that enables AI ASICs—such as Google’s TPUs—to accelerate Homomorphic Encryption (HE). At the time of publication, CROSS achieved state-of-the-art NTT throughput and energy efficiency, being the new SoTA acceleration solution for HE among all commodity hardwares (CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs). The artifact includes standalone, reproducible scripts for every experiment in the paper to support Artifact Evaluation. Please navigate to the jaxite_word folder and follow the README for detailed instructions. TPU access for evaluation can be requested through HotCRP; please contact the authors for credentials and allocation details.

Beyond reproducibility, this artifact provides a curated, community-friendly workflow to help new users: (1) request free TPU resources, (2) set up the CROSS software environment, (3) build a clear conceptual understanding of HE fundamentals, and (4) perform practical performance profiling and debugging. We are committed to maintaining CROSS, incorporating new features, and responding to community needs. Contributions are warmly welcomed as we work toward the shared goal of democratizing high-performance, cryptography-based privacy protection.

metadata.title: Evaluating Internal Mechanisms Artifact
metadata.description:
Evaluating Fuzzing Internal Mechanisms Via Internal State Variables

This repository contains the artifact for the paper “Evaluating Fuzzing Internal Mechanisms Via Internal State Variables” (ICST 2026).

The paper proposes a methodology for evaluating fuzzing internal mechanisms using internal state variables, rather than relying solely on aggregate outcome metrics such as overall coverage or total bugs found. The artifact supports this methodology by providing tooling, data, and analyses that expose and quantify how fuzzers internally allocate effort and generate results.

The artifact includes:

  • Lightweight instrumentation and Docker-based environments for running fuzzers and collecting internal state variables.

  • Post-processing scripts for computing correlations and utilization metrics from raw fuzzing logs.

  • Precomputed datasets and Jupyter notebooks that reproduce the statistical analyses and visualizations reported in the paper.

Artifact Contents

The repository is organized as follows:

  • fuzzing/
    Docker-based fuzzing framework and experiment configurations. This directory contains:

    • Fuzzer and benchmark setups for the evaluated fuzzers, including AFL++-based variants, EcoFuzz, TortoiseFuzz, and their power-schedule and search-strategy variants described in the paper.

    • Lightweight instrumentation to record internal state variables such as seed selection order, assigned energy, mutation counts, and coverage of generated seeds.

    • A dedicated README explaining how to build base images, coverage builders and runners, and how to launch fuzzing campaigns.

  • scripts/
    Post-processing and analysis tooling, including:

    • Python scripts for parsing instrumentation logs, computing internal state variables, correlating them with fuzzing outcomes, and generating intermediate profiles.

    • A README with instructions for setting up coverage runners, configuring paths, and running the setup and analysis phases of the pipeline.

  • report/
    Jupyter notebooks implementing the analyses and visualizations corresponding to the paper’s research questions:

    • R1_Correlation.ipynb: Correlation analyses between internal state variables (e.g., assigned energy, selection order) and fuzzing outcomes (e.g., coverage).

    • R2_R3_Mutation.ipynb: Analyses of mutation utilization and utilization ratios, corresponding to RQ2 and RQ3.

  • results/
    Precomputed datasets used by the notebooks, including:

    • Aggregated coverage results over time for each fuzzer, variant, and benchmark.

    • Inputs and outputs for internal-state-based correlation analysis (RQ1).

    • Data for mutation utilization analysis (RQ2).

    • Data for utilization ratio and efficiency analysis (RQ3).

System Requirements

The artifact has been developed and tested primarily on Linux using Docker-based isolation.

  • Operating system: Ubuntu 22.04 (other recent Linux distributions may work but are not officially tested).

  • Docker: Version 23.0.3 or newer, with the docker group configured, the user added to that group, and sudo/root access available for setup steps.

  • Python: Version 3.8 or newer.

  • Jupyter: Any recent Jupyter environment (e.g., JupyterLab or classic notebook).

Additional Docker and fuzzing-specific prerequisites are documented in the fuzzing/README file.

Usage Overview

The artifact supports two primary usage modes.

A. Inspect and rerun analyses using existing data (recommended for quick evaluation):

  1. Install Python and Jupyter.

  2. Open the notebooks in the report directory.

  3. Execute the notebooks; by default they read from the precomputed datasets in the results directory.

  4. The generated figures and tables correspond directly to the results reported in the paper.

B. Reproduce fuzzing experiments from scratch (time- and resource-intensive):

  1. Follow the instructions in fuzzing/README to build Docker images, compile coverage builders and runners, and launch fuzzing campaigns.

  2. After fuzzing completes and raw logs are generated:

    • Configure paths, fuzzers, and benchmarks as described in scripts/README.

    • Run the post-processing setup phase to parse logs and extract internal state variables.

    • Run the analysis phase to generate processed results.

  3. Point the notebooks in the report directory to the newly generated results and re-execute them to reproduce all analyses and plots.

Mapping to the Paper

The artifact mirrors the structure and evaluation workflow of the paper.

  • Fuzzers and variants correspond to the 14 configurations evaluated in the experimental section.

  • Instrumentation and scripts capture the internal state variables defined in the methodology, including assigned energy, selection order, mutation counts, and coverage per seed.

  • RQ1 (Correlation Analysis) is implemented via the correlation scripts, corresponding results directories, and the R1_Correlation notebook.

  • RQ2 (Mutation Utilization) and RQ3 (Utilization Ratios and Efficiency) are implemented via the mutation analysis scripts, corresponding results directories, and the R2_R3_Mutation notebook.

Together, these components allow reviewers and researchers to inspect the proposed internal-state-based evaluation methodology, reproduce the main quantitative findings, and optionally rerun subsets of the fuzzing experiments to validate robustness.

metadata.title: OML-vect: Enabling Automatic Compiler-Driven Vectorization of Transformers
metadata.description: This is the supporting artifact for the paper titled ”Enabling Automatic Compiler-Driven Vectorization of Transformers” as published in CGO 2026. It includes the source code for the proposed tool (oml-vect), along with scripts to compile and reproduce all experimental results presented in the paper. We provide a Docker image containing all necessary dependencies preinstalled, enabling straightforward setup and execution of the experiments. The setup supports running the experiments on an x86 host, and it also allows cross-compilation for RISC-V ISA, and it automatically transfers the statically linked RISC-V binaries to the host to be then copied to the RISC-V target via scp. The reported results were obtained on Intel Xeon an x86 64 Intel(R) Xeon(R) E5-2630 v4 CPU @ 2.20GHz and a Xilinx U55C FPGA emulating an Atrevido 423 RISC-V 64-bit core with a 512-bit vector unit
